blocks.x: Let's come over and get our names on here. We'll get your name first.
Mitchell McCallister.
Let me see, we're recording this in Natchez, Mississippi, right here. This is your place of business, your ballroom.
Yes, sir.
And grocery store, too.
Yes, sir.
Well, why don't you sit down and make yourself... Sure, sure. Relax. And Harry, put your name on here, too. Yeah.
This is Harry Oster.
Gwelma, you want to come along? Good past you. Yeah. Gwelma Brown. And Bob.
Rita Oster.
And Dick Allen.
Yeah, we've got all our names down here.
Now, let's see, what's today's date? This is March...
19th, I guess.
March of 19th, 1960. Where were you born, Mr. McAllister?
Uh, Natchez.
Right here in Natchez. And what kind of music did you hear when you were quite young?
I heard guitar.
A lot of guitar around here. I heard music.
Madelon. Violet. Pian.
Do we get your exact age now, you might not ask?
Ooh, 78. You've got a right good age, huh? Did they have any trumpets or clarinets or saxophones or trombones when you were young?

No, sir. The first one came in here was the colored fellow by the name of Frank Brakely. He played trombone. Trombone was first. Then the little short cornet. And then people began to add sax. And Bud's son, I know he ran away from the band at one time, and he decided he would, he thought within himself that he would learn to play sax. And he got on his father and warned him to learn him sax. To buy him a sax, at least. And his father gave him a sax. And he was just, he mastered that for just, he wasn't a month.
He was reading a little, and he got to be a perfect wizard on that side.

And from then, well, he had chased away from home for a while and came back and met lots of musicians, different places, and he looked over the billboard and we would get in. Next was a trombone and there's a trumpet player. And on and, you know, like that, till the band got to about 18 strong. And we never had been out no more than just serenading and playing for little country clubs and little dances like that. Mrs. Trevi Poole was a white lady of us dancing school. She gave us our first dance here in Natchez. I think at the Institute Hall. And we made a dollar man that night. And we thought that that was just lots of money. And from there we serenading, serenading around amongst every night then to be a bunch of white gentlemen and ladies would get us to go for little parties and things. And he was just a gifted singer. I imagine it just came to him just, he was, he could thunder. Absolutely. He could sing. He'd be on the bluff and people would be dancing over the river. By his, he could just, he could sing. He'd sing a few little, little old small megaphone, you know.
Oh, yeah.

Yes, like that. He wasn't awful. It had to have been this. No telling you, you're going to hurt him in New Orleans. And so that's the way the band began to, then he began to play in Vidalia, to Ferdy, St.
Joe, Newton, and all around in a different place like that.

And then, after quite a bit, Mr. Peabody, he came south here and we were in New Orleans at the pub, the Haymarket, St. Charles, but there wasn't any colored oxys in there during that time. Well, we went into New Orleans. They were carrying the excursions by the river at that particular time, you know. There's those, oh, excuse me, I could have gotten rid of that.
It's okay.
By the steamboat. So there was about, I think there were four boats in the pretty, pretty heavy orchestras.
What year was that? How did you carry?
I can't exactly recall now, but it was back in the Longin steamboat times, when the excursions was coming up the river, you know, down by the big excursion boats then.
Oh, I see. Did you ever hear any of the songs the Roustabout sang on the river, loading and unloading? Things like Alberta, let your hair hang old?

I remember that, but who knows who can I. Well, of course, we practiced that. We were all upstairs at all times. And so they're taking us into New Orleans. And we got into the St. Charles Hotel. And they had a heavy orchestra there. And they had us dressed like the old farmers with the big hats and the overalls. And so we went in there. And now, the first had taken us out to the riverfront. We got in there just a little before the big boats got in. And all the big heavy orchestra was cutting up out there in the water. Well, you couldn't get in. You couldn't hardly see the front town there. It was crowded with lots of people. So we was out just about, I guess, two and a half, three blocks. And we cut out out in that water out there, sir. And the mayor of the town had to stop Bud from singing. They were pushing the people over in the river. The people was coming so right. You mentioned New Orleans, hasn't you? You seen that riverfront? They were shoving them in the river. He called him Jim Scott. He said, you'll have to stop that Jim Scott. That fella could thunder. And we went on up from there to the banana shed, from there to the St. Charles Hotel. And we went in the dance pavilion. We sat up. We were dressed like farmers. And a couple of the laws there, they said, well, where did that tasty man came from? Well, we sat up in that time when we cut down in there and thundered and the people and the doing the carnival. And they just had to stop Bud from singing and playing in New Orleans at that particular time. From then on, why did it?
Did you do any country music?
Well, just a few things that we used to use, like Bill Bailey and and some time. How does that some time go? Do you remember any of the words of it?
I think that it's sometime you caused me to wonder.
Sometime you caused me to wonder. But, boy, it's been so long now since I played anything. What year were you born again?
Let me get this straight. March the 15th, 1882.
March the 15th? Happy birthday. Happy birthday.
Almost. That's right. Just a amen. Very. How were you when you took up music?

I was on the river, dishwasher, on steamboats at that particular time. And there were a fellow, the cook was a mandolin player. Just a little round mandolin. And I could, had the guitar and I used to kind of just plunk along, play, you know, just for myself. And he, he says, I have a guitar. I said, can't you play a guitar a little bit? I said, I saw that. I thought I saw you uptown one day playing guitar. I said, no, I wasn't playing. I just had it sitting around the barbershop there and just enjoying myself and keep it coming in, trying to learn. And he said, well, bring it down on the boat sometime. And I carried it down there and I didn't know anything about being the thing. He'd say, G, F, D. Show me how they, you know, chord.
And well, I learned pretty good.
And that's the way I started playing the guitar. That was the old time guitar then. And then from there to mandolin, banjo mandolin.
Did you use the two fingers or a pick or four fingers?

I used this hand for picking all four fingers. I recall, all the charts, flats. How many fingers did you use the pick with? No, not playing. I was just only complimenting him behind his, uh, mandolin there. He was playing mandolin.
Did you use a thumb pick or a flat pick? Just a flat pick.
Just a flat pick. Just a flat pick.
Just a flat pick.
I never could use a thumb pick. I had a pretty fast wrist. But you never used your fingers? Only just chording.
Just in chording in your left hand.

Yes sir. Oh no, not now. You played band style. There wasn't anything. We had to do old band style. There wasn't anything like. Compliment? No, yes, just compliment. Not the pick and nose. Just only complimenting behind him. So I never was, uh, doing any picking, you know, leading or anything. Learning anything. You know, on one myself. You know, I always, I always compliment.
What was the first tune you ever learned?
Bill Bailey, won't you please come home. I never will forget that.
And about how old were you then?
I was about, uh, eighteen. Between seventeen and eighteen.
It's an old song. It's an old song.
Bill Bailey is an old song.
What, uh, when do you think you heard what seemed to you to be jazz? Do you have any idea? The earliest time?

Well, no sir, I don't. After I let the music along, I got the, you know, young fella getting wild and I, uh, sit up by being a, I guess, pretty quiet fella here in my hometown. I don't know, it seems like that, uh, if I have to say it with you gentlemen, sure, that, uh, I was a pretty quiet fella and I was pretty well liked by all of the white people. I never had anything very much, but they always made things convenient for me. But I was just a straightforward colored fella and up until this present moment now. I never had no big jobs to pay very much, but I made quite a bit of money. And all that was gave to me. It was gave to me by your people, so it's no use in me saying anything against that. They would gave me, get out of anything. Mitch, what do you think you can do? Well, what do you want? We'll open up your place. But I was a straightforward fella with it. I done right. They gave me everything.
Did the bands and that just play like they did down in New Orleans? Yes, sir. Same kind of music.
Same kind of music, jazz, when his voice began.
What did you call it when you first heard it? Did you call it jazz or what? Yes, sir.
Yes, we named it jazz. You first heard it saying anything?
Jazz.
That's the way it came, jazz.
Would that be 1900 or 1910 or 1920 or some other date or what?

Let's see 19, just about 19, 19, 1912. Let's see. Yeah, we was playing jazz because we were doing the high water. We were over here at this right, right. You see this bakery, a wholesome bakery. And they, they, they, they, they placed us out there to play for the, you know, the people out the high water. And they, you know, over there. So it's about in 1909, 1910. Because I was playing about, yes, about between, three and.
Well, if you were able to play, excuse me, when you were 18, then you were learning to play it 1900, about then, 60 years ago. Oh yes, ma'am.
I was playing at that time.
Yes ma'am.
I was playing at that time.
What instruments did you have when they had that high water?

Just the guitar, just the playing string guitar. Not the, just the playing the old six strings. No, I'm talking a band is what I mean. Well, we had, uh, two guitars and voice. Three malons and a, two malons and a violin. Six of us, I think. Yeah, just six. Was that violin? Two guitars, yes, that was both. I started with him.
You started with him, huh? How many years were you with him?
Forty-three years.
And when did Bud start adding the horns, trombones and barons?
The first... Trombone.
You said a trombone was first.

Trombone was first, then the cornet, then the cornet again, and then the clarinet, and the violon. Then his, uh, Walter King, a boy from New Orleans, a Chinaman, a Chinaman. And he married his daughter. He was a violin player. What year was the trombone? What year was the trombone came in, though?
About what time? Would that be before World War I or after?
Let me see.
That was during World War I. During World War I. During World War I. The trombone. The trombone came in. That's right.

I remember. So it was mostly all strings up until that time. So it was mostly all strings up until that time. We didn't have any wind at all. But it was mostly all strings up until that time. That was only his voice. Oh, yes. It was.
It was all strings up until that time.

It was all strings up until that time. We didn't have any wind at all. But only his words voice. That was plenty, I guess. Plenty of words. Did Blood ever play any instrument at all? Yes, sir. He was added to the mallow. Oh, I didn't remember that. Yes, sir. He was added to their mallow section. Yes, sir. He was added to their mallow section. He was in the mallow. Three. But he just, you know, had to remember it to their mandolin section. Yes, he was in the mandolin. There was three. But he just, you know, played a while.
Did you have those potato bug mandolins?
That's right. That's right. That was the one.
That's the one with the round back?
The round back, that's right, with the stripes on it.
Did they ever have any five string banjo players around here?
Well, hmm, sometime later they had quite a few. Then Percy came in, and I think that Percy came in, had, I think Percy was with Harry Walker.
Out of Alexandria?
And he, he went up to country, and I just, I have, he was with this boy out in New Orleans a while. Oh, just, I thought, hmm.
What instrument does he play?
Percy?
No, the other guy from New Orleans, you were talking about.

No, he had an orchestra in here then, there were two brothers, um, what was the boy's name? Heavy Dark Boys. Heavy Dark Boys? Yes, one, fli- What instrument? Flips. Uh, uh, uh, trump, uh, trumpet. I think the brother did. Yes, I know those fellas well, too, used to come in here quite a bit, go in here with him.
Well, we'll ask Percy about it when we go in.
Percy, where you find Percy? Percy can tell you how great he is. You say Percy's in Villeplatt now. He's in Villeplatt with, with Otis. Otis Smith.
Yes, Otis Smith.

And, uh, I think Percy's, he's playing, uh, he's playing piano now. But he was, well, he was stringing instrument all the way around because he, from guitar to banjo, and, uh, he tried to play bass a little, but now he's strictly, he's, he's playing piano. Playing piano now together. I thought that, uh, I was thinking that they'd be up here, I think one, one night next week, if I'm not mistaken. But, uh, you could, uh, go up on Franklin Street, uh, a boy works in the Savoy Grill by the name of, uh, Daley. And Daley could tell you when, that he would be in there. I think that he's, uh, sponsoring a dance out at the Horseshoe Circle. Or you could call anyone that's connected out there in the Horseshoe Circle. And I think they, they gave him, because they came here and told me, he says, uh, uh, one of the boys was in here, his father passed last week. And he told me, he says, uh, Mitchell said, we want you when we come out to see how David Hawkins has changed from, uh, he and I was, used to play guitar together and banjo. And, uh, he, uh, he's changed now. He said, he's just one of those. And he told me, I said, I want you to come out to see. But after my people got sick, I just didn't have any help, so I had to stop to help those. And, uh, that fire just, just taking all the run out of me, I just, just forgotten it. And, uh, maybe if I hadn't got a pretty good job, I'd have maybe been trying to baffle around, trying to play the music until, yeah.
Well, you were in the fire itself.

I just came out of notice I wasn't there. I had gone out just across the, just across the street, just a block, just across the street. And when I sit there and we drink, uh, I think we drank a, I drank a beer, I think it was beer and something. But then I got excited and they were eating some, a sandwich and cold drinks. When we came out, people was just yelling, screaming. And we stayed on the other side. It was about, you know, half a block, you know. It was just wide, it was that intersection, you know, right there. So that, uh, quiet things. We didn't have to go over there. And the fire department came in and was throwing the water so, and jumping. People just, I don't know, just fierce. They had them out, I guess, they were all the way across the street. They almost, uh, the cars couldn't pass. They were dragging their people right out in just, out in the street. And the cars couldn't pass. They had to stop, had to stop the traffic. And all along the walk, or just having to step between, you know, people looking for their mothers, and for their children, brothers and sisters. Just a block, huh, on both sides, you see. Couldn't have to pass. Try how to carry traffic around. The law did. Now those boys, I'm thinking that they'll be here, um, one day, next week.
Well, we'll leave you a phone, won't we? Uh huh.
So, okay.

If she can take the message, if I'm in, I might come back up again, some other weekend. We also would like to find some guitar players around here, to record our, guitar players, banjo players, all kind of people we're looking for.
I see.

We'll be interested both in, uh, well, the old ones, who may not be good players now, but who have interesting old songs, or a style of playing that people no longer use. That'll be interesting. Or, if we find some younger people, who are still exciting, then, uh, we might be able to put them on a record, actually, too. There's that possibility. We've done that in a few cases. Oh, I see. We find, uh, sometimes people, uh, no one is heard of, who have a lot of talent, and... That's right. ...we have friends, and recording companies, and we put out some records ourselves, and some of them get to be fairly well known after a while. That's right. So, if you know of any, uh, really talented people around, we could probably help them.
Okay, sir, they're more than great.
Yeah. That's right, sir.

I'm more than great. I think I know a couple of boys, they just practically done. They retired now, has little jobs, but they're pretty bright after all. They, they pick up one, you know, sometime, in different places, and, you know, do lots of... They've got pretty good voices, and they memorize pretty good, too. You know, I'm pretty good about a whole lot of things they say. They don't have to read or anything, just so long as they've got the talent. I understand they've got the talent. I said, well, I never, just myself, that, uh, you know, I never was much of a reader myself. But, uh, they gave me credit for being about one of these. Whenever I, you showed me something, I made it, and then I could thunder with one of them. I didn't just... They could just hear me above them all, you know. And I learned how to call, just full calls, well, my, some flats, sharps, and so forth. Well, I got those, too, and everything like that. But it seemed like to me that they would always want me... I had to get a heavy wrist. And, uh, with full calls, gave plenty of harmony. That's what Bud liked, because you had to give it behind him. Maybe then he'd drown you out with his voice.
When Bud started out, what did he sing in those times?

Bud sings, Meet Me Tonight in Dreamland. And, uh, Bill Bailey, won't you please come home? And, uh, sometime, you cause me to wonder. Uh, Diana? Oh, I had a list here, or if I knew, I had a list here, and, uh, oh, I, I could just sit here, and if you'd come to me just in a little while, I could tell you something all night long, but... Well, we'll come back. And, uh, I think that, uh, but I'll tell you who can, who's... If you don't, how long will y'all be here?
Well, we're gonna leave tomorrow, but we can come back.

Well, we'll, we'll, we'll come back. I have a, there's another, uh, friend of mine here that, uh, that plays, uh, he's done retired now, too. He was with us, Louis Mazik. He says, I'll call him tomorrow. What is your... At least I go out to his home. He's the only one. What is your... That... Sax. Yes. And, uh, he's done retired now.
When did the saxophone get the pop-up order on you? About...
Let's see. I don't know exactly... I don't know exactly when. The day, the date or the year even down. I don't know.
After... Was it before the First World War or after? Or during?

After the First World War, because we didn't have... And, uh, during the First World War, the band was... I know we were all eligible then for the Army. And we didn't stay. And, uh, just, I guess, a year or two later, Sax began to come in, because his son was just getting organized into the band. And that's just about the time, I guess, a few years later before, he gave his son a saxophone.
Is his son still here?

He got destroyed in the fire. I didn't know that. That, that, that was this band, the band. And, uh, his madam, she won't take it over and handle it. But, uh, now Griffin, the boy here now that, going in the band playing piano, he's here. He's working, uh, just, he's entertaining. He can sing, and he work by himself. He do mostly all the, uh, jobs and, around here now, right now. He's here. He's about your size. Not as big as Bud, though, huh? Not quite as big as Bud. There's lots of people thought that he was playing piano when, uh, after Percy was playing guitar. Then he'd taken piano. He wasn't quite as big as Bud. There's lots of people thought that he was Bud's son. But he wasn't. He's here now, and, uh, I don't know why he's... He's entertaining somewhere at some of these clubs here now.
Well, did, would you say that Bud weighed 250 pounds? Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Much better than me.
How much did you say blood weighed now?
Around two something. I just remember now.
Well, bigger than me. You have to be...
But you weigh about 230 or 240?
About 220.
And it's a little bit heavier than you. 10 pounds, 20 pounds? Just about, I guess, around 10, 12 pounds more than you. 5, 260, yes. I think that's what...
Was he tall as me?
About your belt. Height, yes.
Did they play any blues in those times?

Blues, yes, sir. We had, I think, two, three different blues. And... I don't know, I had some of those... Quite a few of those recording here that Mr... Oh, my gentleman. That his son was a writer, too. He came here. And I gave him lots of stuff. I guess that's about the way y'all found my name at, I guess. I missed...
Well, she got it from Griffin's brother, huh?

Griffin's brother. Tom Griffin's brother. His brother. Come see. Oh, yes, ma'am. Well, hi. And Mr... He used to... He used to... He was here and his father used to handle their potato chips and so forth. I think he lives... He passed, though. He is. Is this your home here?
This is my home, but I don't remember.

He was on the corner of Union. He was on the corner of Union and... Oh, Miss Cora. Huh? What is that... You know where that colored boy is working for him now? His son came here and... And... We'll talk... Where? For who? The potato chip. You know, that colored boy was driving... Mr. Simmons. Mr. Simmons' son came here. He's a writer and... Oh... You know Mr. Simmons? Mr. Simmons. Yes. Mr. Simmons. Yes. That's right. He was here. And he and I sit out there and we talk... I guess about two, three hours out there. And he's got lots of stuff, if you know what he's at, he can tell you about. And I've got to memorize lots of stuff that I told him. And I think he went... He was talking to Griffin. See? Griffin was one of the latest fellas that came in with us that, you know, could play piano. We were shocked to a piano player. He... Got killed.
Did you ever make any records yourself?
No, sir.
You know what Bud did?

I think that we made some records and... What's the name of it? Uh... Through Fidelio over to... John... And... And... Through Fidelio over to... John... And... North from Johnville over to... Uh... Anything. I forget. Like you're going across the Red River, they're going into Bunky, coming from Baton Rouge, what's the name of that time? Is that around... Elec... Not Elec... Around Alexander.
Alexander. Yeah.
Coming in from Bunky to Alexander, that's right, Elec. That's right.
He made some records around Elec. Yes, around Elec, yes.
Were they put out?
I don't know, sir.

I never did... But... Bud, I think Bud called up for that time or two about those records, but... I don't know how... What's the trouble? Why he didn't get an answer? If he did, why, if there's anything, he got that himself. He didn't ever let us know much about that.
Did any of the men with Bud's band going up north and make good? Up there? Or did they stay here?
They all stayed here. Yeah. They all stayed here.
I'd like to know the names of some of the... Some of the players that played with him.
Pretty much passed out. When the band first started, it started with... Willie Holmes.
What instruments?

Bass. Charlie Laverton. Madeline. Madeline. Fred Pogginhorn. Madeline. Bud Scott sang. Double Down Madeline. Ed Shaw. Guitar. Mitchell McAllister. Guitar. That was the band consistence. Six of us. Six of us played at some time. Well, there'd be seven. One of the boys could get away. They had no wind in it. There wasn't much in there at all at that time.
By the way, did you ever know a fellow named Douglas Williams? He played around Mississippi on three, four, clarinet played?
I'm thinking that one... If we had Douglas here, I'm thinking if that was the same Douglas, he'd kill you. He did, huh?
Is that the guy that sort of played a slap-down clarinet? You know, the...
Something like that.
Like funny noises, chicken crows?

Yes, he could play that. He was out of New Orleans. He was out of Baton Rouge. He came from Baton Rouge here with us. You remember when... You're going to remember. Douglas got killed on North Pine, Pine and Woodlawn. How long ago was that? Oh, it's been quite a bit. Just bubble up the colored boy that used to work for, uh, Williams and Williams. Now, he didn't get, you know, not fighting. He got killed by an automobile. Well, we used to have a store on the corner of Pine and Woodlawn. Well, right... We had it there until 1949, about. He was right there, the colored lady that made the pie. Yeah, right? Just coming out of her place. Uh-huh. Yes, ma'am. Miss Luc... Lucille? Yes, ma'am. We got in the way. And, uh, he was crossing the street. I don't, I don't know whether Mr. Brown was there with his store at that particular... I don't think Mr. Brown was there. Of course, y'all was... Yeah, y'all, yes, Mr. Yes. Well, then, uh, he got killed crossing the street right there. This one of these, of course. Were killed by a... William and Williams, uh... Um... Um... Um... Um... Um... Um... Um... I think it... Right there.
Coming out of Miss Lucille. Well, that's Charlie McCurtis. Got killed by the embalming drug here. I thought that was Charlie... Brundy. Yeah, Walter Brundy.
Walter Brundy.

Walter Brundy. And that's what you said? Yeah, he took lessons from Charlie McCurtis. He was a drum and he was playing baronet and he came over. That's Brundy got killed by the... Well, that's what you...
Didn't you say Brundy? No, I was thinking about Douglas Williams.
Oh, Douglas.

Yeah. Oh, Douglas. No, he... Douglas... Why did... Hmm... No, why did... Tell him to Douglas. Douglas died someplace. I don't know what became of Douglas. It went away or went somewhere. Douglas and... I don't know what became of Douglas. It went away or went somewhere. Douglas and... Douglas and... Douglas' friend... He's... He's with... He's playing bass now with... With Otis. That came here with... With... With him. I just remember... I went away. I went to Chicago and I... I think when I came back, Douglas had died. I don't know. Well, Brundy...
What was he doing here? Brundy? Uh-huh.
He's playing clarinet. With who? With Bud.
With Bud.
With Bud.
With Bud.
Yes, with Bud.
Yeah. And he'd given up drums entirely.

I don't know. I didn't know where he... He told me he used to drum sometime, but he came here... Well, he played with some great band. Oh yeah, Brundy was... That's a good clarinet player. He came here playing good. Very nice clarinet.
He used to play with the Superior Band, Bunk Jonte.
Yes.
I know you've heard of Bunk.

Yes. I said, I'm at the Spallestown. And Brundy was good. That's right, I was thinking about Douglas. I don't know. I think... I don't know whether Douglas died here, but when I came here with Douglas had been dead. I know after the band, I went away. I didn't know what... I didn't know too, but I just done forgotten right now.
When were you in Chicago?
Always been quite a while since I was in Chicago. So I've been here in this place for 20 years.
Was that before the Pressure that you were in Chicago?
Sure. And...
It was after the First World War or before? Yeah.
After the First World War.
After the War and before the Pressure.
Yes, I think that's... We were saying... Practically the whole band was eligible for First World War I and... Well, the White folks, yes. Yes, I'm mighty. Kepa Shelf. Yes.
What kind of music did you hear in Chicago?
Well, I never gone very much to music.
You didn't hear King Oliver, Doe Armstrong, any of those fellows? Well, yes, I heard them.
Up in Chicago or here?
Say? Did you hear them here or up in Chicago?

Well, I heard them in Chicago. Quite a bit, but... I mean, I'm paying. I had forgotten it, at least let it alone. Some of them I like, you know, lots of music. I think they got pretty good swing music. Pretty good. Coming into jazz at that particular time, I was very keen, as I thought, within myself. Just practically, I know of it. It was a lot of quality to me. I... Some of them I hadn't heard the swing that they had, you know. They were changing just fast. And then it just... Things just went then, you know. Every time you... You hear something, it's just different and different. So... You didn't know what to take for the best or not, so it was pretty hard to get out. Some of them same... I noticed that some of them played the same piece and they just like quite a few old timers now. Here now, it's just... Well, I never heard... Sometime I don't know even what to... Even singing until they name on the name and... When they... Swing it. Sometime they just... Play it, try to... Straight along the thing. Sounds very nice, but...
Did you ever go to the Dreamland or the Royal Gardens in Chicago or the Deakin Theatre or any of those places like that?
Yes.
Do you remember who was playing in the Dreamland or the Lincoln Gardens or the Royal Gardens plantation?

What was that one time? What was that? What was that? We were just talking about that in here the other day. Just last week, Tom and I was trying to... Was thinking about that same thing. We left with Mr. Peabody, I think from... From West Baden, Indiana. And... We gone over there. Let me see, I don't know. I just remember now who was playing that dance at night.
Did you ever hear Erskine Tate up there? No. No. No.
No, sir.
No, sir. No, sir.
No, sir. No, sir.
No, sir.
No, sir.
No, sir. No, sir. No, sir. No, sir.
No, sir.
No, sir.
I don't know about the Maple Leaf, yes. I don't know about the Frog Lake, I can't remember. It might have been that, but it wasn't that Frog Lake here.
I think that's James Scott or Scott Joplin. I can't remember which one. I think it's James Scott wrote that, you know. Scott Joplin wrote Maple Leaf and so many other
good ones. Easy one is one of my favorites. That's a pretty hot number.
Did you ever hear anyone sing a song about Jelly Roll, Jelly Roll, Forever On My Mind?
Jelly Roll. If I didn't, I can't record.
You made my poor mother crazy, you drove my poor daddy blind. Is that what the words I think? Mm-hmm. Original Jelly Roll Blues and the Jelly Roll Morton up in Chicago.
It seems like...
Just a set of words to that...

And it seems like that... It seems like that I wouldn't say now, you know, to be pretty going on it, but it seems like to me that I heard someone saying something about that. I heard parts of it somewhere. Oh, you did, huh? It seems like I did. Remember about when? It must have been a long time ago. Oh, yes, it was quite a bit ago. I can't recall now, but it seems like to me that, as you said, I got a mother on my mind. Well, they got two, three of those kind of good...
Yeah, that's been in several times, you see? Oh, yeah, yeah. Yes. Uh, what about dancing? Did you ever dance much yourself?
Well, it's pretty good. That's pretty good one time.
Well, when you were young, what dances were they doing around here?
Two-step. Waltz. Sharks. Swing out and all those kind of things that we never needed. And the thing about that, the round dances were played for those, the round dance, you know, figures.
What about mazookas? Did you ever do any mazookas?
Well, I didn't. I didn't like it. I was pretty good, but I never did.
You didn't like the mazookas?
No.
Other people dance the mazookas?
Oh, yes. All those. Quadrille? Name, yes. They had the quadrille there. Yes.
Did you ever do anything they called a contra dance? Contra dance?
Country dance.
Country dance. Country dance.

I just swing out, first lay it on the head, lead off the right. Yeah, square dance. Square dance. I guess quite a bit of that. But I never did play it from anyone, but I never did. I never could learn it. I just, I didn't like it. Somehow.
I wonder who some of your favorite musicians were on the various instruments? Like, who would be your favorite guitar player?
Percy was good.
Percy was mighty good, huh?
Pretty good. Percy was good.
What about a trumpet player, sir?

Well, we had a cellar of those. The same boy which you just called. But I told you that I didn't know where he was. You called his name and I said he was, I don't know when he left. Here he... Douglas, where do you call him? Douglas. That's right. I think Douglas was good. Good. Was a paronet player? Good. He was, yeah. He was Douglas. He was a trumpet player.
Douglas was a trumpet player.
Yes.
And, uh, what about trombone?
Trombone. He played trombone.
Who did you like on trombone though, here?
Well, now, uh, we, we, we, we had just after, after trombone came, it was late. And then after trombone passed, I never got any, I never got any trombone player.
Who was the...

Of course, the band was beginning to, you know, but he was pretty well passed, had passed. And, uh, the boys didn't, couldn't get along with, uh, the manager that they had. And, uh, so that caused a bunch of the boys to, anywhere they could get, get a job while they just went and looked for him, tried to get him.
What about saxophone? Were there good, good saxophone players around here?

Yes, we had a bunch. Louis Musique, he was a good saxophone player. He was here. The doctor's father was a doctor. He's out in the hall. And, uh, we had, uh, Bud's son was, practically, he was a wizard on saxophone. He was just about the goodest we ever had here. Or anyone ever came in here on saxophone.
What about Walter Barnes? Now, how would he compare with those fellows?
Well, Walter Barnes, he could play saxophone. He was, he was good. Well, he was just fine on sax. I thought I did.
Who was the best singer?

Uh, Bud was just about the best around here. And, uh, we had, uh, a boy used to sing with them. We had a quartet. I was singing tenor. Bud was leading. Walter King was, uh, singing baritone. And H. Shaw was, uh, H. Shaw was singing baritone. And, uh, his son was singing, uh, bass. We had a pretty good quartet. But, uh, singing, uh, we ain't had anyone around here that could be Bud singing.
I was wondering about some of the people that used to play with Walter Barnes back around 1928 or 29. Do you remember Cicero Thomas? He's a trumpet player?
I met him a couple of times, yes.
Was he from here?
Cicero, no. I don't think Cicero was. George Dick then? You know him? I met them too. Neither one of them wasn't from here.
Where was Walter Barnes from?

Now, such me. I wouldn't know. He came in here in a time or two, but a couple of Augustus. And the last time he came in here, he came in here just by himself. And, uh, he was loafing. And, uh, he played a few dances here with us. And up and then we gone, even to Jackson. And, uh, Joe Black, uh, sensation, a drummer used to be at Rappersfield. He had an orchestra, uh, there.
Is that Joe Black or Joe White?

Joe, uh, Joe White. I said, I'm sorry. That's right, Joe White. And, uh, he was short of, uh, two, three boys. Well, he was just, he was just loafing with us. So we let, uh, him have him. And he joined him and, uh, the boys began, he began to, I guess search the billboard and he found out why there was a bunch of loose musicians that was, uh, and he began to gather them in, you know, one, one or two at a time, write them and place them in, set them in. And that's why he, he broke up the band in his, in Jackson. So, uh, that's the way I liked it. Yeah. Yeah.
What did Walter Bond play mostly?
Sax.
Mostly tenor or alto or what?
He played tenor sax.
Did he play any clarinet?
I don't know whether he doubled or clarinet or not.
Mostly tenor.
Mostly tenor. Every time I seen him, he was playing sax.
Do you remember Ed Burke or Bradley Bullock? They were trombone players with Walter Bond? I don't know. What about, uh, Lucius Wilson? He played tenor.
I met him.
But he wasn't from here, huh? No. He had a couple of alto players, Irby Gage and Wilson Underwood.
I met all those fellas, but I, I, they.
What do I just want to check? Paul Johnson, a piano player?
I met those two.
But again, not from Natchez. Not from Natchez. And Blanca Hall was a banjo player. Not from here. Lewis Thompson bass?
Lewis Thompson bass. Lewis.

He played tuba, I'm not. Yeah, he probably even played Mighty Fine tuba. And Bill Winston drums. No, you don't remember those? Well, it's nice to know I never could quite get those guys lined up. There's so many Mississippi musicians. What bands passed through Natchez from other towns that you'd hear?
Not recently. It hasn't been. Oh, but, uh, I, I don't know.
Well, I don't mean late years. I mean the whole of the town bands.

Oh, all of the bands out of New Orleans, they were here. And out of Batting Rouge, Toots and all those boys. Toots, John McKenna. John McKenna. I was up in this way time after time. And, uh, other than that, they just little, you know, small bands come in, different things, and had much of it. It seemed like they had very little pedigree, you know, just dropping through, low, some stick around a while.
Would they have a battle of music here?
Well, not very much.
Not too much.

Not too much. Not then. Not then. I think that night that, uh, when I was doing it at Spire, well, we just cut in, you know, just as a musician has come to town, and we knew him, and the boys went out to let him meet the girls. Well, we'd sit in, you know, and pick up wherever I was about to trumpet player, pick up the trumpet, or bring my trumpet, and that's, that's the way. I'll tell you about, but a very few bands came in here during Bud's time, Bud taking care of everything. That practically that, from carnival and all, and big dances, and practically all the swell dances that you were, in fact, in this district.
How far away would you travel?
Well, we'd go through, around to Oklahoma.
Oklahoma, that far away?
Yeah, California, and up west, west Bayton, around the Yawlands, and Mobile, all around, you just, we just.
Would you go up north Mississippi or much?

Oh, yes, oh, through north Mississippi, well, I'll tell you. I think there's a bunch of that stuff back there now. Bud had their chances to go most anywhere. Princes, dukes, queens, kings, he offered jobs, and, uh, but during that time, they warned him for such a limited time to come in, and we had met great musicians, told him, said, if you want to just make this augustry just like it is, and get away from here, say, you make some money. But Bud was here, and he was getting along all right, and he was, as long as he was getting all right. Sometimes he'd get a little salty, and a couple of letters would get out of his pocket, and a couple of boys would pick him up. He wouldn't tell us once, but we knew it though. He had chances to meet all the people. Now, because that, if his buzz band couldn't get away, but he could get away, that's all right.
Okay.

He could get away. He could have been, I guess, we played dukes, the queens, and, uh, I know that myself, but, uh, and could have been gone some out of this country for a number of times, of course. I might not have been with him, I might have had better musicians than me, or, but, I know that I've had the chances.
Who were some of the New Orleans musicians that came in here?

Well, we didn't have, pretty much all of those boys would, was in Bud's band, was self-made boys right here. Uh, Brundy, he came in here once, and, uh, what's the other part? Uh, what's this called? Uh, what's this called? You called his name, and, uh, uh, the boy I told you was down there playing bass now, came in here with, uh, playing trumpet.
He played trumpet here, and he's playing bass?

No, no. Yeah, well, yeah, he's playing, he's playing bass now with, uh, with, uh, Orlis at Villeplatt, but he came in here with the boy, I told you, uh, uh, was dead. Uh, there's two of them was dead, you know. Uh, well, we talked about him a few minutes ago. Yes, uh, well, now they, them two boys came here together. Uh, and, uh, one's dead, and, uh, the other one's in, uh, he was trumpet player, but now he's playing, uh, bass. Forces, the banjo and guitar.
Jeff Matthews, huh? Would that be Jeff?
No, it's not Jeff. Uh, Jeff played trumpet.
Jeff played trumpet and he died.
No, this boy's living now. What did his brother play? It wasn't a brother, they were friends.
Oh, I see.

They came off Rabbit Foot, I think they came from the Rabbit Foot Show in here. Douglas and the trumpet players. Both of them were trumpet players. He was trumpet players but now he's playing bass for Otis and Vildplatt. Poise played guitar, banjo, now he's playing piano. He has another boy, you know, just got one arm. He's trumpet player too. Now he's doubling on trumpet and trombone.
We play trombone with one arm.
So that's why I told you that they would be up here next week and wanted me to hear whatever. Well, we'll contact him. The good August that he has. But I know.
Well, it's about to run out. We want to thank you a million for this. That's what it's worth. You do appreciate it.
There's lots of that that I would just practically done forgotten now.

We don't come to you as soon as we get the machine apart. That's always the way. I've recorded a lot of groups and they're usually rather stiff while they're playing. As soon as I start to put the equipment away everybody springs into life and starts to play like Wanda playing it. You can stop it.

segments.chapter: Opening and Natchez beginnings
segments.title: Opening: names, place and date of the recording
segments.summary: Interviewers record names at McAllister's ballroom and grocery in Natchez on March 19, 1960.

segments.chapter: Opening and Natchez beginnings
segments.title: Born in Natchez; first music heard and first horns in town
segments.summary: McAllister was born in Natchez, heard guitar young, and is 78. The first horn player in town was trombonist Frank Brakely; Bud's son later mastered sax.

segments.chapter: Opening and Natchez beginnings
segments.title: Bud's band grows to 18; first dance and Bud's big voice
segments.summary: The band grew with new horn players, played country clubs and parties, got its first dance from Mrs. Poole, and Bud's huge singing voice carried over the river.

segments.chapter: Opening and Natchez beginnings
segments.title: Excursion steamboat engagement in New Orleans
segments.summary: The band went to New Orleans for the riverfront excursions and the St. Charles Hotel, dressed as farmers; crowds got so heavy the mayor stopped Bud singing.

segments.chapter: Opening and Natchez beginnings
segments.title: Country music, Bill Bailey and interviewer's birthday
segments.summary: Asked about country music, McAllister recalls Bill Bailey and Sometime You Caused Me to Wonder; birthdays are exchanged.

segments.chapter: Learning guitar and early jazz
segments.title: Learning guitar on the steamboats; first tune Bill Bailey
segments.summary: As a dishwasher on steamboats he learned chords from the cook, played flat pick and mostly accompanied in band style.

segments.chapter: Learning guitar and early jazz
segments.title: Getting along with the white community in Natchez
segments.summary: McAllister describes himself as quiet and well liked by white people who helped him get work.

segments.chapter: Learning guitar and early jazz
segments.title: When and how jazz arrived in Natchez, c. 1909-1912
segments.summary: They called the music jazz; he dates it around 1909-1912, playing for people during the high water.

segments.chapter: Bud Scott band instrumentation and repertoire
segments.title: The early six-piece string band with Bud
segments.summary: The band had two guitars, mandolins, violin and voice, six players; McAllister was with Bud for forty-three years.

segments.chapter: Bud Scott band instrumentation and repertoire
segments.title: When trombone, cornet, clarinet and sax joined the band
segments.summary: The band was all strings until the trombone, cornet, clarinet and violin came in, about World War I; Bud also played in the mandolin section.

segments.chapter: Bud Scott band instrumentation and repertoire
segments.title: Banjo players, Percy and other local musicians
segments.summary: Banjo players came later; he talks about Percy, now playing piano with Otis Smith in Ville Platte, and points the interviewers to Daley and the Horseshoe Circle.

segments.chapter: Bud Scott band instrumentation and repertoire
segments.title: Surviving the fire
segments.summary: McAllister describes the fire he was across the street from and the chaos of people looking for family; it took the wind out of his music.

segments.chapter: Bud Scott band instrumentation and repertoire
segments.title: Interviewers explain their collecting and ask for leads
segments.summary: Oster says they want old players and young talent for recordings and ask for local leads.

segments.chapter: Bud Scott band instrumentation and repertoire
segments.title: His role as rhythm guitarist supporting Bud
segments.summary: He was no reader but a loud full-chord guitarist whose heavy wrist and harmony supported Bud's voice.

segments.chapter: Bud Scott band instrumentation and repertoire
segments.title: Bud's early repertoire
segments.summary: Bud sang Meet Me Tonight in Dreamland, Bill Bailey and Sometime You Caused Me to Wonder; McAllister promises to remember more.

segments.chapter: Bud Scott band instrumentation and repertoire
segments.title: Saxophone comes in after World War I and Bud's son
segments.summary: He places the sax a year or two after the war, when Bud's son got one; the son died in the fire and Griffin now plays piano.

segments.chapter: Bud's band: records, members, Douglas and Brundy
segments.title: Bud's size
segments.summary: They compare Bud's weight and height to the interviewers, about 250 to 260 pounds.

segments.chapter: Bud's band: records, members, Douglas and Brundy
segments.title: Blues and the writer who visited earlier
segments.summary: They had a few blues; he recalls Mr. Simmons's son, a writer who talked with him for hours and also spoke with Griffin.

segments.chapter: Bud's band: records, members, Douglas and Brundy
segments.title: Bud's band records near Alexandria
segments.summary: McAllister never recorded, but Bud's band made records somewhere near Alexandria; he never learned if they were released.

segments.chapter: Bud's band: records, members, Douglas and Brundy
segments.title: Original members of Bud Scott's band
segments.summary: Nobody went north; he lists the original six, with Willie Holmes on bass, Ed Shaw and himself on guitar.

segments.chapter: Bud's band: records, members, Douglas and Brundy
segments.title: Douglas Williams, the clarinetist killed by a car
segments.summary: Asked about Douglas Williams, he recalls a slap-style player from Baton Rouge who was killed crossing Pine and Woodlawn.

segments.chapter: Bud's band: records, members, Douglas and Brundy
segments.title: Walter Brundy and confusion with Douglas
segments.summary: They sort out Brundy, a good clarinetist who had played drums and with Bunk Johnson, from Douglas, whose fate McAllister cannot recall.

segments.chapter: Chicago and the wider jazz world
segments.title: Time in Chicago after World War I
segments.summary: He lived in Chicago after the First World War and before the Depression, long before settling in Natchez.

segments.chapter: Chicago and the wider jazz world
segments.title: Hearing King Oliver and Louis Armstrong; changing jazz styles
segments.summary: He heard them in Chicago and reflects on how fast jazz changed into swing.

segments.chapter: Chicago and the wider jazz world
segments.title: Chicago clubs and traveling with Mr. Peabody
segments.summary: Asked about Dreamland and Royal Gardens, he recalls traveling with Mr. Peabody from West Baden, Indiana but not who played.

segments.chapter: Chicago and the wider jazz world
segments.title: Ragtime tunes and Jelly Roll Morton lyrics
segments.summary: Interviewers ask about Erskine Tate, Maple Leaf Rag and Jelly Roll; he vaguely recalls hearing the words.

segments.chapter: Dance, favorites and Walter Barnes
segments.title: Dances of his youth
segments.summary: He lists two-step, waltz, quadrille and square dances, but disliked mazurkas and country dancing.

segments.chapter: Dance, favorites and Walter Barnes
segments.title: Favorite guitarists, trumpeters and trombonists
segments.summary: Percy was the best guitarist and Douglas a good trumpeter; trombone playing faded when the band's manager fell out with the men.

segments.chapter: Dance, favorites and Walter Barnes
segments.title: Best saxophone players, including Walter Barnes
segments.summary: Bud's son was the best sax in town; Louis Musique and Walter Barnes were also good.

segments.chapter: Dance, favorites and Walter Barnes
segments.title: Bud as best singer and the vocal quartet
segments.summary: No one could match Bud, and the band had a quartet with McAllister singing tenor.

segments.chapter: Dance, favorites and Walter Barnes
segments.title: Walter Barnes's men and the Joe White orchestra
segments.summary: He met Barnes's trumpeters, none from Natchez; Barnes loafed in Natchez, then joined Joe White's band in Jackson.

segments.chapter: Dance, favorites and Walter Barnes
segments.title: Walter Barnes's instrument and sidemen
segments.summary: Barnes played tenor sax; the interviewers run through his sidemen, and McAllister met most but knew none locally.

segments.chapter: Touring, visiting bands and close
segments.title: Bands passing through Natchez
segments.summary: New Orleans and Baton Rouge bands came through, few stayed, and there were no battles of music.

segments.chapter: Touring, visiting bands and close
segments.title: Touring range and Bud turning down offers
segments.summary: Bud's band traveled to Oklahoma, California and Mobile; Bud turned down chances to leave, preferring to stay in Natchez.

segments.chapter: Touring, visiting bands and close
segments.title: New Orleans musicians who came to Natchez
segments.summary: He recalls two trumpeters from the Rabbit Foot Show, one dead and one now bass with Otis, and other musicians around Ville Platte.

segments.chapter: Touring, visiting bands and close
segments.title: Closing thanks
segments.summary: The interviewers thank him and end the recording.
